'''Patricia Davies''' ({{née}} '''Owtram'''; born 19 June 1923) is an English former [[Cryptography|codebreaker]] who served as a special duties linguist in the [[Women's Royal Naval Service]] during [[World War II]]. She and her younger sister [[Jean Argles]] are often referred to as "The Codebreaking Sisters".<ref name="Royal British Legion">{{Cite web |title=Codebreaking sisters of WW2 {{!}} Royal British Legion |url=https://www.britishlegion.org.uk/stories/codebreaking-sisters-of-ww2 |access-date=2023-06-23 |website=The Royal British Legion |language=en}}</ref> As a teenage interceptor, Davies listened to radio transmissions in both German and encrypted code as part of the British [[war effort]], transcribing and decoding the messages and passing them on to [[Bletchley Park]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Lyall |first=Sarah |date=2024-03-08 |title=Move Over, Alan Turing; Meet the Teenage Girls Who Rocked Bletchley Park |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/03/08/books/review/enigma-girls-teenagers-bletchley-park-candace-fleming.html |access-date=2024-03-09 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

After the war, Davies was a television producer, journalist, and author. She was also an organiser of the [[Chiswick]] [[Women's Institute]] and a patron of the [[Sea cadets|Sea Cadets.]]<ref name="Chiswickw4">{{Cite web |title=Chiswick's Local Web site |url=http://www.chiswickw4.com/default.asp?section=info&page=patdaviesbletchleybook001.htm |access-date=2023-06-23 |website=www.chiswickw4.com}}</ref><ref name="Royal British Legion" /> Until Argles died in 2023, the sisters were the last to have been required to sign the [[Official Secrets Act 1939|Official Secrets Act]]. In their later years they discovered that each had been doing top secret war work. In their nineties, they appeared frequently on radio and television relating stories of their wartime activities. Their book ''Codebreaking Sisters: Our Secret War'' became a best seller.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Dunlop |first=Tessa |date=2023-05-04 |title=Jean Argles obituary |language=en-GB |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2023/may/04/jean-argles-obituary |access-date=2023-06-23 |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

== Early life ==
Dorothy (née Daniel) and Carey Owtram had three children, Patricia, Jean, and Robert. Carey Owtram owned a cotton mill in [[Bolton|Bolton, Lancashire]], and the military-minded family lived in a large, countryside, sandstone house belonging to Carey Owtram's father.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Argles |first=Jean |date=2021-11-11 |title='The war bumped me out of my sheltered life and made me feel more important than ever before' |language=en-GB |work=The Telegraph |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/women/life/war-bumped-sheltered-life-made-feel-important-ever/ |access-date=2023-06-23 |issn=0307-1235}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Hamnett |first=Gillian |date=2021-11-02 |title=November: War & Remembrance |url=https://autumnvoices.co.uk/general/november-war-remembrance/ |access-date=2023-06-23 |website=Autumn Voices |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref name="Legasee">{{Cite web |title=Patricia Davies |url=https://www.legasee.org.uk/veteran/patricia-davies/ |access-date=2023-06-23 |website=Legasee |language=en-GB}}</ref> After being homeschooled, the children were sent to boarding school for a few years, Patricia Owtram leaving at 17 years old. In the 1930s, the Owtram family also employed an Austrian [[Expulsions and exoduses of Jews|Jewish refugee]], Lilly Getzel, as a cook after she left Austria escaping the [[Nazism|Nazi dictatorship]] there. Patricia Owtram enjoyed spending her evenings with Getzel, who could not speak much English, and so Patricia learned enough of Getzel's native German language to achieve conversational fluency and proficiency in German. This helped her later in her interview for the [[Women's Royal Naval Service]] (WRNS). In 1939, Patricia Owtram gained her [[School Certificate (United Kingdom)|school certificate]]. As the war started, Dorothy Owtram, who had driven a truck for the [[Women's Land Army]] in the [[First World War]], became an [[Air Raid Precautions]] warden. In 1941, Carey Owtram, having served in the [[Army Reserve (United Kingdom)|Territorial Army]], went to the Far East with his regiment. After the [[fall of Singapore]] in 1942, he was imprisoned in Japanese [[Prisoner of war|POW]] camps until the end of the war.<ref name="Owtram-2020">{{Cite book |last1=Owtram |first1=Patricia |title=Codebreaking Sisters: Our Secret War |last2=Owtram |first2=Jean |publisher=[[Mirror Books]] |year=2020 |isbn=978-1-913406-05-9 |location=London |language=en}}</ref>

== Career ==
===War service===
In 1942, age 18, Patricia Owtram joined the WRNS.<ref>{{Cite web |title=BBC Radio 4 - Last Word, Anne Perry, Dame Mary Quant, Jean Argles, Ahmad Jamal |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/m001l2k6 |access-date=2023-06-23 |website=BBC |language=en-GB}}</ref><ref name="Royal British Legion" /> When it was discovered from the results of a WRNS German test that she spoke good conversational German, she signed the Official Secrets Act<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Bletchly |first1=Rachael |last2=Baron |first2=Olivia |date=2020-07-23 |title=WW2 codebreaking sisters kept jobs secret from each other for 30 years |url=https://www.lancs.live/news/lancashire-news/ww2-codebreaking-sisters-lancashire-kept-18646278 |access-date=2023-06-23 |website=LancsLive |language=en}}</ref> and, after two weeks of basic training and a further intensive specialist interception course, was promoted to [[petty officer]] and started work at the British navy's signals collection sites, called [[Y service|Y stations]], around the coast. These stations were called Y, phonetically standing for WI, which in turn stood for "Wireless Intercept".<ref name="Owtram-2020" /> They were where secret German military communications were intercepted, transcribed and, if in a code other than [[Morse code|morse]], passed on to [[Bletchley Park]]. Owtram's first post was in [[Yorkshire]]. She later transferred to [[Lyme Regis]] in 1943 as [[chief petty officer]], and then to [[Dover]] (opposite [[Cap Gris-Nez]]) where she turned 21 two weeks after [[Normandy landings|D Day]]. In Y stations, the WRNS worked in twos, round the clock, transcribing German military communications between ships, in the North Sea, the Baltic, or the Dover Straits depending on the regularly varied postings, and which were, for example, between ships and their base or between commanders and groups of ships.<ref name="Great British Life-2020">{{Cite web |date=2020-05-04 |title=Meet the Codebreaking Sisters who helped bring Victory in Europe |url=https://www.greatbritishlife.co.uk/people/22610254.meet-codebreaking-sisters-helped-bring-victory-europe/ |access-date=2023-06-23 |website=Great British Life |language=en}}</ref>

Later she worked for the [[Supreme Headquarters Allied Expeditionary Force]], in London under General Eisenhower, scanning German official documents to search for potential [[war criminals]].<ref name="Great British Life-2020" /> She was offered a job as a translator at the [[Nuremberg trials]] but, at her mother's request, went home to be with her father who had returned after surviving his ordeal as a POW.<ref name="Legasee" />

===Civilian work===
After the war, Davies was assistant archivist at the British embassy in Oslo, Norway. She studied English at [[University of St Andrews]], graduating with a [[first class honours|first class]] [[undergraduate Master of Arts]] (MA Hons) degree.<ref name="Lady Mother">{{cite news |title=Credit Where It's Due: The Long, Strange Tale of Patricia Owtram and The Lady Mother |url=https://issuu.com/somervillecollege/docs/somerville_magazine_2023_-_issuu/12 |access-date=16 April 2026 |work=The Somerville Magazine |volume=2023 |date=28 August 2023 |pages=12–13 |language=en}}</ref> She then undertook research on ''[[The Lady Mother]]'' by [[Henry Glapthorne]] at [[Somerville College, Oxford]], [[matriculating]] in 1951.<ref name="Lady Mother" /><ref name="Honorary Fellow" /> She graduated from the [[University of Oxford]] with a [[Bachelor of Letters]] (BLitt) degree in 1953.<ref name="Lady Mother" /><ref name="Honorary Fellow">{{cite web |title=Centenarian Codebreaker Pat Owtram Becomes Honorary Fellow |url=https://www.some.ox.ac.uk/news/centenarian-codebreaker-pat-owtram-becomes-honorary-fellow/ |website=Somerville College |publisher=University of Oxford |access-date=16 April 2026 |date=28 March 2024}}</ref> Her [[Doctoral advisor|supervisor]] was Arthur Brown, an academic of University College London as no suitable Oxford academic was available.<ref name="Lady Mother" /> When her edition of ''The Lady Mother'' was published by the Malone Society in 1959, it was attributed to Brown with no mention of her; this academic injustice was only rectified in 2023.<ref name="Lady Mother" /> After Oxford, she held a study fellowship as an exchange student at [[Harvard University]].<ref name="Lady Mother" /><ref>{{cite web |title=Remembering the Somerville Women of World War Two |url=https://www.some.ox.ac.uk/news/remembering-the-somerville-women-of-world-war-two/ |website=Somerville College |publisher=University of Oxford |access-date=16 April 2026 |date=10 November 2024}}</ref>

She was a journalist in [[Manchester]] for a time and a television producer for the then newly established [[ITV Studios|Granada television.]] She was involved in the production of programmes such as [[Coronation Street|Florizel Street]] (now known as Coronation Street), and was key in developing other well known programmes such as [[University Challenge]], [[The Sky at Night]] where she worked and travelled with [[Patrick Moore]], and [[Ask the Family]]. She retired in 1983.<ref name="Chiswickw4" />

In 2017, the Owtram sisters published the wartime diaries of their father, Colonel Cary Owtram, under the title of ''One thousand days on the River Kwai: The Secret Diary of a British Camp Commandant''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Private Papers of Colonel H C Owtram OBE TD DL |url=https://www.iwm.org.uk/collections/item/object/1030021106 |access-date=2023-06-30 |website=Imperial War Museums |language=en}}</ref> This led to their giving talks at book festivals, and making radio and TV appearances.<ref name="Owtram-2020" /><ref>{{Cite news |last=Kelly |first=Guy |date=2018-08-09 |title=VJ Day anniversary: 72 years on, how our father's PoW diary reveals his heroism |language=en-GB |work=The Telegraph |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/family/relationships/vj-day-anniversary-77-years-fathers-pow-diary-reveals-heroism/ |access-date=2023-06-28 |issn=0307-1235}}</ref>

In 2020, Pat Davies and Jean Argles published ''Codebreaking Sisters: Our Secret War'', a book about their own wartime experiences, written under their maiden name of Owtram.<ref name="Owtram-2020" />

== Awards ==
Davies's war service was recognised with the [[Victory Medal (United Kingdom)|Victory medal]].<ref name="Chiswickw4" />{{citation needed|reason=According to our article (per wikilink), this is a World War I honour. Please confirm what medal or honours she actually received.|date=April 2025}}

In 2009, the [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour]] government under [[Gordon Brown]] awarded the women who worked at Bletchley Park a Bletchley Badge.<ref name="Chiswickw4" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Osborne |first=Bridget |date=2019-06-17 |title=Pat Davies receives France's highest honour – Chiswick Calendar |url=https://chiswickcalendar.co.uk/chiswick-woman-receives-legion-dhonneur/ |access-date=2023-06-30 |website=The Chiswick Calendar |language=en-GB}}</ref>

Davies name is on a brick in the wall at Bletchley Park honouring those who worked in connection with the place.<ref name="Chiswickw4" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Codebreakers' Wall, Patricia Owtram (Davies) |url=https://bletchleypark.org.uk/codebreaker-wall/?index=107&section=A1 |access-date=2023-06-29 |website=Bletchley Park |language=en-GB}}</ref>

June 2019, Davies was awarded the [[Legion of Honour|Légion d'honneur]], Military, the highest order of merit in France.<ref name="Great British Life-2020" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Second World War veterans receive Légion d'honneur |url=https://uk.ambafrance.org/Second-World-War-veterans-receive-Legion-d-honneur |access-date=2023-06-29 |website=France in the UK |language=en}}</ref>

In 2019, she was also granted the freedom of the Borough of [[Chiswick]] where she resides.<ref name="Chiswickw4" />

In 2024, she was elected [[Honorary title (academic)|honorary]] [[Fellow (Oxbridge)|fellow]] of her alma mater, [[Somerville College, Oxford]].<ref name="Honorary Fellow" />

== Personal life ==
Throughout the war, the two Owtram sisters wrote letters to each other. Since both had signed the Official Secrets Act and had been involved in top secret work, it was not until the 1960s and 1970s, and after the publication of material about the work of [[Bletchley Park]], that the two sisters talked to each other about their war work and discovered the similarities in their war experiences.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Owtram |first1=Patricia |title=Codebreaking Sisters: Our Secret War |last2=Owtram |first2=Jean |publisher=Mirror Books |year=2020 |isbn=978-1-913406-05-9 |pages=291 |language=en}}</ref> Their parents never knew anything about the top secret war work that their daughters had undertaken.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bletchly |first=Rachael |date=2020-07-22 |title=Sisters signed Official Secrets Act and never told parents of remarkable actions |url=https://www.mirror.co.uk/news/uk-news/ww2-codebreaker-sisters-kept-incredible-22399532 |access-date=2023-06-23 |website=mirror |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Benson |first=Rhianna |date=2021-11-14 |title=Meet the Lancashire sisters who both broke top-secrets code during World War II |url=https://www.lancs.live/news/lancashire-news/meet-lancashire-sisters-unaware-were-22135385 |access-date=2023-06-23 |website=LancsLive |language=en}}</ref>

Patricia Owtram was married to Ray Davies, a  BBC journalist.<ref name="Chiswickw4" />

Still giving talks in 2023, to, for example, older groups in the [[University of the Third Age]] (U3A), Davies wrote, "It usually raises a laugh when I tell them that I may be the only old lady in Chiswick who knows how to use a [[Sten|Sten gun]]." (p.&nbsp;292)<ref name="Owtram-2020" />

== Legacy ==
Details of Davies's life and work were recorded in ''Army Girls'' by [[Tessa Dunlop]],<ref>{{Cite book |last=Dunlop |first=Tessa |title=Army Girls |publisher=[[Headline]] |year=2021 |isbn=978-1472282088}}</ref> published in 2021, and in both ''The Bletchley Girls'' 2015<ref>{{Cite web |title=Female codebreakers: the women of Bletchley Park |url=https://www.historyextra.com/period/second-world-war/female-codebreakers-women-bletchley-park-tessa-dunlop/ |access-date=2023-06-23 |website=HistoryExtra |language=en}}</ref> and ''Elizabeth and Philip''  2022 by the same author.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Dunlop |first=Tessa |title=Elizabeth and Philip |publisher=[[Headline]] |year=2023 |isbn=9781035402427 |location=London}}</ref><ref name="Armistice day" />

A portrait of the two sisters holding a telegram from their father was painted by Dan Llywelyn Hall.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-08-15 |title=Meet the two codebreaking Lancashire sisters who played important roles in war |url=https://www.lancashiretelegraph.co.uk/news/18651099.meet-two-codebreaking-lancashire-sisters/ |access-date=2023-06-23 |website=Lancashire Telegraph |language=en}}</ref>

There are seven films about Pat Davies in the Veterans Video Archive.<ref name="Legasee" />

On [[Armistice Day]] 2022, aged 99, Davies joined Andrew Pierce and Tessa Dunlop for an interview about her wartime experiences.<ref name="Armistice day">{{Citation |title=Armistice day: World War 2 Veteran Patricia Owtram joins Andrew Pierce | date=11 November 2022 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=99TmIL5gk1g |access-date=2023-06-23 |language=en}}</ref>
